name: Ephedra and ephedrine
short: A meta-analysis of 50 trials found 2.2- to 3.6-fold higher odds of psychiatric, autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms and palpitations; rarer serious events rest on poorly documented case reports.
text: A meta-analysis of safety data from 50 controlled trials of ephedra or ephedrine, often taken with caffeine, estimated 2.2- to 3.6-fold increases in the odds of psychiatric, autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms and heart palpitations; the trials were too small to draw conclusions about events occurring in fewer than 1 per thousand users, and most of the case reports were too poorly documented to assess. A later meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials of ephedra-containing oral medications found no significant difference in adverse effects between treatment and control groups. A case-control study found no association between ephedra use at any dose in the 3 days before the stroke and haemorrhagic stroke (adjusted odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.32 to 3.11); for daily doses above 32 mg the odds ratio was 3.59 (95% CI 0.70 to 18.35), and the authors concluded that ephedra is not associated with increased risk except possibly at higher doses. Both confidence intervals are wide, so neither estimate is precise. A review of adverse event reports classified 57 of almost 1800 as serious psychiatric events (such as psychosis, mania or severe agitation, and suicide attempts); two-thirds involved people with pre-existing psychiatric conditions or use of other mood-altering medicines or illicit substances, and the authors concluded that these case reports do not prove a causal link but raise concern that one may exist. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
